title: Test Your Survey on Synthetic Respondents Before You Waste a Single Real One
summary: How to do this easily with Expected Parrot
body_text: Test Your Survey on Synthetic Respondents Before You Waste a Single Real One How to do this easily with Expected Parrot John Horton Jul 15, 2026 tl-dr; If you run consequential surveys, you should be testing them with simulated respondents ahead of time to identify problems with the survey at both a technical level and a research question/conceptual level. Expected Parrot makes it easy to do to this. I was once involved in fielding a survey to software developers about their AI tool usage. The survey asked if they user had used “GitHub Copilot”; the survey methodologist we were working with had never heard of this and edited it to just “GitHub” assuming we had a typo. We missed his edit and as a result, nearly 100% of our developers reported “Yes.” Oof. Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work. I think nearly researcher who has run surveys knows this feeling: the data comes back, and a question that seemed clear turns out to have meant three different things to three different people; a skip pattern didn’t work right; a scale confused everyone; nearly everyone selected “other” which is not what you planned. By then it’s too late. You’ve wasted money & time. Even if the survey is fine, there is the similar feeling of “ah, we should have asked X” once you actually start doing the analysis. Cognitive testing / piloting are great but… The known defense against this kind of failure is piloting and “cognitive testing”: run the survey past some real people first, watch where they get confused, and fix it. The problem is that good cognitive testing is slow and expensive. If done with a convenience sample, it also requires someone playing a role—actual target population of a survey—and it’s not likely we really understand this population with respect to the question (if we did, we probably wouldn’t be asking). AI gives us two nice options to this slow, expensive and unrepresentative problems. We can now use AI to proofread a survey. Frontier models have some good practices “on distribution” i.e., they know a survey shouldn’t have a double-barrelled question. They know that people will tend to choose middle options and so on. Suppose you are surveying customers and you draft this: Q7. How satisfied are you with the support you’ve received? ○ Very satisfied ○ Satisfied ○ Neutral ○ Dissatisfied ○ Very dissatisfied You can give this to a frontier AI. Claude, for example, nails the issues : But here’s the rub: If I am editing a survey on Qualtrics or Survey Monkey, how, exactly, do I get Claude to review? Maybe Qualtrics has some homebrew AI tool but it’s likely behind a paywall you’re on the wrong side of. And suppose it makes some nice fixes, how can I deploy my survey? Not being able to deploy it forecloses an exciting option in design. We can have AI simulated personas take our survey. To the extent those respondents are realistic, we can even analyze the data they return to pilot / stress test our whole analysis flow. But if I want to have simulated personas try out my survey, how do I do that? Do I give “them” a link to my survey? Paste the survey text into chat and the persona? How do I get the data out? I can ask Claude to simulate, but it will just “one shot” a plausible-seeming distribution of responses not actually have a model pretend to be a given persona. If I want to do more sophisticated analysis on the responses, am I manually downloading a CSV giving it to Claude Code? If I learn something, I need to go back to Qualtrics or Survey Monkey. It sounds like a flow-breaking hassle. And more importantly, it breaks the survey design process into distinct design & test phases where instead it should be happening at the same time. Imagine programming computers but you can only test the code you’ve written it and it’s expensive to do so. The Expected Parrot Approach We’ll use the Expected Parrot Research Agent as a design studio for our survey. It’s a conversational agent so you can just paste in what you want to do: The research agent asks a bunch of clarifying questions to understand my intent and goals: The research agent does not just keep all this in a chat context—it writes Python code in our open source package EDSL to create, in code, the survey being used, the personas being constructed, the data-generated and so on. The personas here are just reasonable guesses but if you have past survey data, something a lot smarter can be done instead. The research agent actually runs these personas through the survey using our API. Critically, EDSL has a standard for all the usual question types so the AI simulation very closely matches what would be send to actual humans e.g., free text, multiple choice, text-box and so on. After this simulation, it finds the same issues as Claude (this is a pretty simple one) but it’s done by those AI personas actually going through the survey. This becomes critical with more elaborate personas, complex piping and skip-logic and so on. It generates a written report on the issues with the “quotes” from synthetic personas: But more importantly, it can make the necessary fixes and then re-test. Here we can see it deals with the “But I haven’t contacted support” issue that had previously caused a simulated subject to select “Neutral”: One we feel good, the research agent can then refine the question and immediately deploy it via email, a URL or even Prolific: You can take the survey here . The research agent can analyze the real survey and/or simulated survey: Under the hood, the research agent is not just drawing on context to all this: it’s writing the Python code to actually analyze the data. This matters because it is easy to analyze more data when it comes in, the research agent (or any coding agent) can reason over what was done and find issues. Concluding thoughts This is a toy case, and you might catch it on a careful read. The point is that a synthetic pass catches it reliably and instantly , across every question at once, for the cost of a prompt—and the harder, subtler versions of these same problems are the ones you’d otherwise only discover after fielding. Some References Beatty, P. C., & Willis, G. B. (2007). Research synthesis: The practice of cognitive interviewing. Public Opinion Quarterly, 71 (2), 287–311. https://doi.org/10.1093/poq/nfm006 Presser, S., & Blair, J. (1994). Survey pretesting: Do different methods produce different results? Sociological Methodology, 24 , 73–104. Presser, S., Couper, M. P., Lessler, J. T., Martin, E., Martin, J., Rothgeb, J. M., & Singer, E. (2004). Methods for testing and evaluating survey questions. Public Opinion Quarterly, 68 (1), 109–130. https://doi.org/10.1093/poq/nfh008 Tourangeau, R., Rips, L. J., & Rasinski, K. (2000). The psychology of survey response. Cambridge University Press. Willis, G. B. (2005). Cognitive interviewing: A tool for improving questionnaire design. Sage. Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

body_text: HNI Corporation Recognized Among America’s Best Companies by TIME July 24, 2026 PDF Version MUSCATINE, Iowa--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jul. 24, 2026-- HNI Corporation (NYSE: HNI) has been named to the TIME America’s Best Companies 2026 list. Presented by TIME and Statista Inc., the annual ranking recognizes top-performing U.S. companies based on employee satisfaction, financial performance, and sustainability transparency. “We’re honored to be named among TIME’s America’s Best Companies 2026,” said Jeff Lorenger, Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Officer of HNI Corporation. “This recognition reflects the strength of our culture, the dedication of our members, and our ongoing commitment to strong business performance, workplace excellence, and corporate responsibility. It reinforces the foundation we've built and our focus on creating long-term value for our members, customers, and shareholders.” HNI ranked #575 on the list of 1,000 U.S. companies recognized. This year, TIME expanded the ranking beyond the previous Best Mid-Sized Companies list to include all eligible U.S. companies with more than $100 million in annual revenue. The ranking reflects performance across three dimensions: Employee satisfaction, derived from survey data from more than 217,000 U.S. employees evaluating company image, workplace atmosphere, working conditions, compensation, and more. Financial performance, based on multi-year financial data evaluating revenue growth, net income, and asset performance. Sustainability transparency, based on publicly available environmental, social, and governance (ESG) information and standardized metrics, including carbon emissions intensity, human rights policies, governance, and reporting practices. HNI's disciplined operational execution, member-driven culture, and commitment to corporate responsibility continue to differentiate the company and drive sustained success. The complete rankings are available at TIME.com . About HNI Corporation HNI Corporation (NYSE: HNI) has been improving where people live, work, and gather for more than 75 years. HNI is a manufacturer of workplace furnishings and residential building products, operating under two segments. The Workplace Furnishings segment is the thought leader in commercial furnishings and the preeminent global designer, innovator, and provider of workplace solutions going to market under unique brands serving multiple channels and customers from the largest multinational companies to small local businesses. The Residential Building Products segment is the nation's leading manufacturer and marketer of hearth products, which include a full array of gas, electric, wood, and pellet-burning fireplaces, inserts, stoves, facings, and accessories. More information can be found on the Corporation's website at www.hnicorp.com . title: I’m 2 Years From Retiring With $810k. A 20% Drop Now Would Hurt More Than One at 75. Here’s Why
summary: An unexpected downturn early in retirement can affect a portfolio differently than the same downturn during your working years.
body_text: When you are close to retirement, every market decline can feel different than it did decades earlier. At this stage, you generally have less time to recover from major losses. While it may be easy to focus on how far the market falls, the timing of a decline can be just as important. A sharp drop shortly before or during retirement could have a greater effect on your savings than a similar loss earlier in your career. Same Loss, Different Consequences Financial planners call this sequence-of-returns risk : A 20% loss at age 50 and a 20% loss at age 66 are the same percentage, yet they can have very different effects. What matters isn’t the size of the drop, but when it happens compared to the time you start pulling money out. A market downturn may be less impactful early in your career because you typically have more time for investments to recover until retirement. You could also continue making contributions during the decline, which allows you to buy additional shares at lower prices. In retirement, a similar decline may happen after you’ve started taking withdrawals. This could then put you at risk of selling investments while their value is lower. The timing of the loss, combined with ongoing withdrawals, can make it more difficult for a portfolio to recover than the same decline earlier in your investing years. What Sequence Risk Could Cost an $810K Portfolio Let’s assume that two retirees each start with an $810,000 portfolio, withdraw $40,000 per year and experience the same average annual return over three years. The only difference is when a 20% market loss occurs. Here’s how both examples compare. Retiree One: Loss Hits in Year 1 Year Withdrawal Return Balance 1 $40,000 -20% $616,000 ($810,000 − $40,000, ×0.80) 2 $40,000 +6% $610,560 ($616,000 − $40,000, ×1.06) 3 $40,000 +6% $604,794 ($610,560 − $40,000, ×1.06) Retiree Two: Loss Hits in Year 3 Year Withdrawal Return Balance 1 $40,000 +6% $816,200 ($810,000 − $40,000, ×1.06) 2 $40,000 +6% $822,772 ($816,200 − $40,000, ×1.06) 3 $40,000 -20% $626,218 ($822,772 − $40,000, ×0.80) As you can see from the tables, Retiree One and Retiree Two start with the same balance, make the same withdrawals and experience the same average return, but the 20% loss lands in a different year. That single difference in timing leaves Retiree Two roughly $21,000 ahead after just three years. This is a simplified example intended to show how sequence risk could affect different portfolios, not a projection of actual investment performance. Whether your specific portfolio could withstand a downturn early in retirement depends on specific factors like your balance, withdrawal rate and time horizon, which a financial advisor may help you evaluate. One Way to Help Manage Sequence Risk A common strategy to minimize sequence risk in retirement is to hold a cash reserve that is big enough to cover one to three years of living expenses. This could help you pay for spending needs during an early market downturn and potentially avoid selling investments while they’re down. A cash reserve may also offer you more time to recover from investment losses before you need to sell them. A financial advisor can help you estimate how much of a cash reserve to set aside and whether this strategy fits your retirement savings, expected spending and planned withdrawal rate. title: Original Owner: ’71 Malibu Went from Family Car to 12-Second Hot Rod in 40 Years
summary: Dan Hawkins was three years old in 1989 but said he remembers his Uncle Greg coming around to his house in a silver 1971 Chevelle Malibu 350 convertible. Both Greg and Bill, the younger of his mom’s brothers, got him revved up for horsepower from an early age. When the Chevelle eventually became Dan’s 23 […]
body_text: Dan Hawkins was three years old in 1989 but said he remembers his Uncle Greg coming around to his house in a silver 1971 Chevelle Malibu 350 convertible. Both Greg and Bill, the younger of his mom’s brothers, got him revved up for horsepower from an early age. When the Chevelle eventually became Dan’s 23 years later, after his two uncles had it, the drop-top Chevy was turning 12-second quarter-miles and taking his family out for ice cream. Dan’s mother, Shari Winstead, was seven years old and with Dan’s grandparents when they bought the convertible new from Lowe Chevrolet in Marlboro, Maryland, in June 1971. His mom recounted walking into the dealership and Dan’s grandmother, Dottie, pointing to the Nevada Silver Malibu convertible across the showroom and calling out, “That’s the one!” Indeed, it was. Just a year later, the young family took the Malibu on a 2800-mile cross-country journey to a new home in the Seattle suburb of Bothell, Washington. Dan’s research decades later confirmed how special the car was. Dan’s grandfather with the Chevelle he’d bought new. Courtesy Dan Hawkins Industrywide, convertible sales had gone into a steep decline in the early 1970s. Just 5089, or 1.3%, of the 387,000 Chevelles made in 1971 were droptops. Despite those figures, that Maryland Chevy dealer had the confidence to order a well-optioned model for the showroom. The ’71 Malibu convertible, which came standard with the 307-cubic-inch two-barrel V-8 and a power convertible top, started at $3362, including a $107 destination fee. Dan’s grandparents bought the Chevelle in Maryland in June 1971. Courtesy Dan Hawkins This one was well-optioned with the 350-cube four-barrel V-8, Turbo-Hydramatic transmission, air conditioning, F41 Sport Suspension, Positraction rear axle (with 2.73:1 ratio), tilt steering wheel, power steering, AM/FM radio, Rally Wheels, and a few other items for a $4589.25 total. Though not shown on the sticker, Dan remembered the car having power-assisted drum brakes. The reproduction window sticker shows a well-optioned convertible. Courtesy Dan Hawkins Pacific Northwest-Bound Not long after landing in the Pacific Northwest, the Malibu went into the garage and remained there for the next 15 years. At that point, Dan’s Uncle Bill, then 16, convinced his parents to let him revive the Chevelle to drive in high school. As is often the case, the high-schooler was not gentle with it. “It was known to have been airborne on more than one occasion,” Dan said. Bill never officially owned the Chevelle, though, and Dan’s grandparents sold it to his Uncle Greg in 1989 for $3000. “Greg began all the overdue maintenance and repairs left over from the heavy-footed younger brother,” Dan said. “He’d take me to a local demolition derby or the fair, and on other rides in the Chevelle.” From the get-go, the cool Chevy instigated young Dan’s interest in cars. He began to ask questions, such as, “What does the ‘350’ mean?” He knew that and much more by 13 years old, just when his Uncle Greg left Washington in the Chevelle to take a job in South Carolina. His stay there was brief, and he moved to Florida, where, within a year, he got into an accident that damaged the Chevelle’s front end. The silver convertible then spent about 12 years in his garage and being taken to different shops for repairs and upgrades. “My uncle did some work himself, but he suffered from chronic back pain, so he often had to pay people to work on it,” Dan said. He saw the car on a visit to his uncle not long after the collision, and, educated by car magazines, the teen offered some suggestions. “I told him that with the front end taken apart, it was a good time to do an engine swap and maybe put in a 700R4 transmission to make it better for the highway.” The Chevelle in South Carolina in 1999, before a subsequent move to Florida. Courtesy Dan Hawkins Greg liked his car-savvy nephew’s ideas. The original 350 small-block and automatic were pulled, and a body shop in Apopka, Florida, replaced the banged-up front sheetmetal, including both fenders, the hood, and core support. Greg got lucky with a swap motor. He’d befriended a Chevy-specialist performance shop owner who’d built up a 402 big-block from a ’71 Chevelle or Camaro. A 0.030-in. overbore brought it to 408 cubic inches. The original customer had bailed on the project, so the shop owner sold it to Greg for the unpaid balance. The prepped motor went in, along with a rebuilt GM 700R4 automatic overdrive transmission. “He got it painted but couldn’t afford to get it across the finish line,” Dan said. “I occasionally visited him, and we’d always make time to see the Chevelle.” Teenage Dan visiting his Uncle Greg in Florida while the Chevelle was a work-in-progress. Courtesy Dan Hawkins From his teenage years, Dan had been asking his uncle about selling the Chevelle to him when he could afford it. Greg told his eager nephew he’d always planned to keep the car but eventually mentioned two conditions under which he would sell it to him. “He told me I had to achieve my dream of becoming a full-time firefighter, and I had to own a house with a garage to keep the Chevelle out of the weather. I think he was trying to figure out a way to make sure I was mature enough to be responsible with it.” Dan admits that, as a young driver, he did not meet the “responsible” criteria. Following a couple of Chevy pickups, he got a Fox-body 5.0-liter Mustang . One reckless-driving ticket later, he sold the ’Stang and went back to pickups. By 2008, Dan was a full-time firefighter for Renton, Washington, a suburb just south of Seattle. He married his middle-school sweetheart, Shawna, in 2012, and the couple lived in a house they’d bought the year before in Mountlake Terrace, a northern suburb. Dan had his dream job and his garage, and he still had his heart set on the Chevelle. Christmas season that year brought a special present. On a phone call, Dan’s uncle offered to sell him the car. Dan still has the original broadcast sheet for the Chevelle. Courtesy Dan Hawkins “I knew the car would be worth more than the $3000 he paid in 1989, and he knew there was a family deal to honor, since he’d gotten that,” Dan said. “When he got the Chevelle, it was running and driving. I’d be getting it in worse shape. It would take a lot of work to get it back on the road.” They agreed on $6000. Greg told the owner of the Chevy shop that a shipper would be coming to pick up the car. Learning the sale price, the man offered Greg $16,000 in cash on the spot. “I didn’t fault my uncle for it. I knew money was tight for him,” Dan said. “I didn’t want the car to come between us. But he said he’d think about it for a few days.” After those few days passed, Dan got the call. The Chevelle was his for six grand. The Chevelle spent over 25 years off the road, so total miles stayed low. Courtesy Dan Hawkins Factory Basics: 1971 Chevelle Malibu The mid-size Chevelle was a hit for Chevy right out of the gate in 1964. Body-on-frame construction and coil-spring rear suspension gave big-car ride comfort, and the Malibu was the popular upgrade trim line. The 1968 redesign brought curvier lines, and the coupe continued to dominate sales. Chevy sold very few six-cylinder Chevelle convertibles and made it V-8-only for 1971, with the base version having the aforementioned 307-cubic-inch engine. Ordering either the optional two-barrel or four-barrel 350 added “Malibu 350” badges to the front fenders, or a “Malibu 400” would adorn the sides if buyers stepped up to the LS3 400, which was really a 402. (And that, Chevy fans know, was the former 396 with a slight bore job from 1970.) The 1971 Z15 SS Equipment option allowed either of the 350s for lower insurance premiums, with the 402 and LS5 454 available as step-ups. Chevrolet GM dictated reduced compression ratios for all 1971 models and began publishing both the familiar SAE gross horsepower and the as-installed net ratings. The 350 two-barrel offered 245 hp gross / 165 hp net, with the L48 four-barrel rated at 270/175 in the Chevelle. The 402 had 300/260 ratings, and the 454 produced 365/285. Appealing design, known reliability, and the wide array of models and option choices made the Chevelle America’s best-selling mid-sizer for 1971. The 387,000 total included 36,000 El Caminos, which Chevy listed as a “two-door sedan pickup” body style rather than a separate model. Ford’s Torino took second place in the segment with 326,500, including 25,000 Ranchero pickups. Chevrolet From Jigsaw Puzzle to “Day 2” Hotrod Having the Chevelle shipped to Washington added a big chunk over Dan’s $6000 investment. The 408 big-block and 700R4 trans were installed, but not much else. “The car was like a roller with a powertrain, but there was no driveshaft, the parking brake didn’t work, and the engine had none of the accessories or carb installed,” he said. “It had to be winched on and off the trailer, and I pushed it inside my garage with a couple of my firefighter buddies. The car was packed almost to the headliner with parts my uncle had removed and new ones he’d bought. It was like being handed a puzzle, but there’s no picture as a guide, and you don’t even know if you have all the pieces.” Dan dug through and sorted everything, cross-referencing shop manuals with photos he found online. He wanted to keep the Chevy’s appearance as his grandparents had bought it, while acknowledging the car’s hotrod heart and spirit. The Chevelle had 67,000 miles showing when he took delivery and by then had spent more than 25 of its 40 years off the road. Dan had additional work done to the big-block his uncle had installed years before. Courtesy Dan Hawkins Replacing the “Malibu 350” badges with original “Malibu 400” badges he’d found and restored was the smallest part of the reassembly that took the better part of a year. Dan wasn’t trying to pass off the car as an original Malibu 400 convertible, though. The real one was mighty rare, with some estimates suggesting just three dozen cars out of the 17,500 ’71 LS3-optioned Chevelles. Rather, he was going for an in-period “Day 2” hotrod theme. Edelbrock’s RPM aluminum heads, EnduraShine air gap intake, and 750-cfm carb already topped the big-block. Dan gave the 12-bolt Posi 3.73:1 gears, installed Mickey Thompson ET rear street tires, and upgraded to front disc brakes. In the cabin, the original bench seat remained, and a floor shifter replaced the column shifter. At age 27, Dan was finally driving his teen-dream car. A few years later, a hit-and-run while the car was parked sent it back in for some bodywork. When the transmission blew shortly after that repair, Dan learned it had been a stock rebuild and not nearly up to the 402’s output. He had it rebuilt to handle 550 horsepower, and though he knew his Chevelle had nowhere near that, getting it dyno-tuned revealed even less than he thought. The Chevelle kept its bench seat but gained a floor shifter and other hotrod touches. Courtesy Dan Hawkins After the intake gasket blew during a dyno run, the tuner suggested bore-scoping the engine. Numbers on the Speed-Pro forged aluminum pistons revealed that the engine builder had chosen the incorrect part number by one digit. The error meant 8.65:1 compression rather than the 10.5:1 Dan believed it had. Rather than change the pistons, the tuner suggested ordering a custom-grind camshaft from Bullet Racing Cams to maximize the dynamic compression ratio. That swap, plus a Holley XP 950-cfm carb, put the engine into peak health, the dyno revealing 333 hp and 475 lb-ft. of torque. A new cam and bigger carburetor unlocked big power, even with low compression. Courtesy Dan Hawkins “The real test of horsepower is on the track,” Dan said, proving that maxim by running five passes at Pacific Raceways in Kent, Washington, all from 12.0 to 12.5 seconds. Using the Chevelle’s 3920-lb. weight with him in it, 3.73:1 axle ratio, and factoring in the density altitude, he calculated 425 flywheel horsepower, which lined up with the dyno’s wheel hp figures. Making New Family Memories for 14 Years and Counting Dan drives his family treasure Chevelle from May through September. He and Shawna will take their sons out for ice cream and to their baseball practices and games, and Dan enjoys turning heads and entertaining his boys by opening the electric exhaust cutouts he installed. “The car does not go out in the rain, ever,” he said. “I got caught in the rain once, and that was about the most scared I’ve ever been driving any vehicle. It would need a good set of all-weather tires just to barely contain it. I also want to prevent rust.” Dan, his wife Shawna, and their young boys out for a cruise in the hotrod Chevelle. Courtesy Dan Hawkins About five years ago, with COVID shutting down local shows, Dan and some friends organized a car cruise around their large residential neighborhood, Gold Creek in Snohomish. They knew there were other muscle cars in the development, and the cruise brought out about 50 cars thanks to Dan’s friends posting on social media. “Everybody came out to their front yards and waved, and there were lots of kids,” he said. “We’ve done it a few times and gotten about the same number of cars.” Dan and friends organized a local car cruise that raised money for a first-responder financial-support group. Courtesy Dan Hawkins The drivers were cruising for a cause, too, raising money for Lionhardt, a local organization that raises money to help support families of ill and fallen first responders. It was started in honor of and named for a Renton firefighter Dan had been hired with, Donovan “Dono” Eckhardt, who died from cancer at age 37. The Chevelle ferried Dan’s brother-in-law and his wife in their wedding, and his most cherished moment was proudly showing the car to his grandmother when it was finished. “She had not seen the Chevelle since my uncle left with it in 1999. I took her for a few rides in it before she passed away in 2024. Those were special family moments.” The Chevelle ferried Dan’s brother-in-law and his wife in their wedding. Courtesy Dan Hawkins Dan Hawkins parking the Chevelle at his grandmother’s house when she saw it for the first time in about 15 years. Courtesy Dan Hawkins Dan with his firstborn son working on the Chevelle in 2016. Courtesy Dan Hawkins Both of Dan’s boys love being around the Chevelle and helping him work on it, and he’s started buying them their own tools. He’s confident the car will remain in the family. “I love driving it, and there’s of course the nostalgia and heirloom factors that make it a forever car for me.” *** Car: 1971 Chevrolet Chevelle Malibu convertible Name: Dan Hawkins Home: Snohomish, Washington Delivery date: June 17, 1971 Miles on Car: About 75,000 The post Original Owner: ’71 Malibu Went from Family Car to 12-Second Hot Rod in 40 Years appeared first on Hagerty Media .

title: 10 Essential health benefits (EHBs): Everything you need to know
body_text: Categories Health Insurance 10 Essential health benefits (EHBs): Everything you need to know By HealthSherpa Share this post A major win of the Affordable Care Act was the inclusion of Essential Health Benefits (EHBs) in all ACA-compliant health insurance plans. Most broadly, Essential Health Benefits are a way to describe ten categories of services that these plans must cover. All Marketplace plans (aka Obamacare or ACA plans) cover the Essential Health Benefits. To see prices and available Marketplace plans that cover the 10 essential health benefits, enter your zip code below. Because of all the available subsidies and cost-sharing reductions, most pay under $21/month for health coverage. You can also call (872) 228-2549 for help enrolling. Essential Health Benefit Categories These ten EHB categories are: Ambulatory patient services (outpatient care you get without being admitted to a hospital) Emergency services Hospitalization (like surgery and overnight stays) Pregnancy, maternity, and newborn care (both before and after birth) Mental health and substance use disorder services , including behavioral health treatment (this includes counseling and psychotherapy) Prescription drug coverage Rehabilitative and habilitative services and devices (services and devices to help people with injuries, disabilities, or chronic conditions gain or recover mental and physical skills) Laboratory services Preventive and wellness services and chronic disease management Pediatric services, including oral and vision care (but adult dental and vision coverage aren’t essential health benefits) All ACA-compliant plans must also include birth control coverage and breastfeeding coverage. This means that any plan that any health care plan you buy off the health insurance Marketplace, either from HealthCare.gov or HealthSherpa, comes with a guarantee that your plan will include coverage for all of the above types of services, even though details on specific services may vary by plan. ACA-compliant plans also cover coronavirus testing. Preventive Care One key thing to keep in mind is that any of the above Essential Health Benefits that are considered preventive care , versus diagnostic care, are also covered at no-cost thanks to the Affordable Care Act. There are 65 free healthcare services guaranteed by the Affordable Care Act in any ACA-compliant plan. This is true of any plan you purchase off the Marketplace, through HealthSherpa, or that you have through an employer who offers ACA-compliant benefits. Preventive care is not always covered by health sharing ministries , short-term insurance , or indemnity plans. Grab our guide to preventive care to learn more. Please remember that you will need to see an in-network provider to receive these preventive services at no cost to you. To see health insurance plans and prices and enroll, go to healthsherpa.com . What are all of my health insurance options? You have several coverage options for plans that cover all of the essential health benefits. Marketplace/“Obamacare” plan. You can enroll in a Marketplace health insurance plan, also known as Obamacare or Affordable Care Act insurance. See plans and prices here . Medicaid. You also may be eligible for Medicaid, depending on your income. You can see if you’re eligible and apply here . COBRA. If you’ve been laid off recently, you usually have the option of COBRA, where you pay the full premium of the same insurance your employer purchased for you. COBRA is typically much more expensive than Marketplace insurance, but it allows you to continue the coverage you already had. Learn more about comparing COBRA with Obamacare health insurance . Medicare. Once you turn 65, you’re eligible for Medicare . Call us to enroll at (855) 677-3060. When can I enroll in Marketplace health insurance? Anyone who’s eligible can enroll in Marketplace health insurance during Open Enrollment, which runs from November 1 to January 15 in most states. If it’s outside of that period of time, you’ll need a Qualifying Life Event , such as losing your insurance or having a child, to qualify. Grab our guide to enrolling in health insurance to learn more.

title: Flip secures $28 million Series A extension to expand new AI-powered capabilities for deskless workers
summary: Flip secures $28 million Series A extension to expand new AI-powered capabilities for deskless workers
body_text: Berlin, Germany, May 21, 2025 - Europe’s leading software scale-up for the frontline, Flip , today announced a $28 million Series A extension. Led by existing investors including LEA Partners, HV Capital, Notion Capital, as well as Roland Berger. The funding will be used to drive targeted advancements in artificial intelligence and accelerate the company’s growth. Unveiled at the company’s flagship Berlin event, Flip Forward, the new investment will support the next phase development of Flip Intelligence ; an AI-powered solution that automates shift planning, knowledge management, feedback collection, and onboarding processes. By combining knowledge transfer with AI-driven automation, it boosts productivity, reduces process risks, and enhances employee engagement, while continuing to deliver significant time and cost savings. Unlike other solutions, Flip’s AI features are fully embedded into the platform, with no need for third-party tools. Founded inside Porsche by then-trainee Benedikt Brand, Flip was born out of frustration with the disconnect between HQ and teams on the factory floor. Its platform is purpose built for companies with a high proportion of deskless workers, who make up 80% of the global workforce, and digitises all touchpoints between these employees and their organisations. Designed to help HR, Communications, Operations teams and deskless workers streamline their daily workflows enabling them to work smarter, save time and focus on value-adding tasks. “The trust shown by our existing investors is a strong signal of confidence. It demonstrates their belief in our mission and their commitment to supporting us on this journey,” said Benedikt Brand, Founder and CEO of Flip. “With this momentum, we’re ready to shape the next era of AI-driven work.” He added: “There’s still huge untapped potential in digitalisation — especially for deskless teams, where AI can significantly boost efficiency and improve both management and worker retention." “We chose to extend our Series A funding because the opportunities ahead are too good to ignore. From unlocking powerful product enhancements to delivering even greater value for our customers, we're all in. Most importantly, we're doubling down on our promise: exceptional service that drives real, measurable efficiency.” Nils Seele, Partner at LEA Partners , commented on the investment: "In the age of AI, the way we access and interact with business processes is fundamentally changing. Long gone are the days of fragmented tools, it's now time to focus on intelligent bundling in a central platform. The Flip team is working on this vision with impressive energy and expertise. That's why we're doubling down on our commitment. We want to enable every employee to work in a radically better way." “Through integrations and the use of AI, Flip is becoming the intelligence layer between an organisation and its people - automating workflows and generally enabling much more efficient and engaged work. We are very excited to be doubling down and making a further investment in the business,” explains Jos White of Notion Capital . In addition to expanding its AI capabilities, Flip is also focusing on global expansion. With international clients such as Sixt Norway, Ben & Jerry’s Australia, the Australian Football League (AFL) and the School of Rock, Flip is already proving its platform delivers real value on a worldwide scale. To support this expansion, Flip has appointed Simon Eck as SVP Global Sales. Eck previously led sales for the EMEA region at Staffbase and brings extensive experience in international B2B SaaS sales. In recent years, Flip has also secured strong digitalisation partners to help close technological gaps within companies. A strategic partnership with the Boston Consulting Group led to the publication of a study in 2024 focused on how to face deskless labour shortage with technology. Since its founding in 2018, Flip has raised over $60 million in total funding and is now being used by more than 500 companies - including leading brands like McDonald’s, Rossmann, Bosch, and Porsche. Developed in close collaboration with its customers, Flip’s platform is backed by a 160-strong team focused on driving innovation. In 2024, Flip acquired UK-based The Bot Platform, formerly a key Meta partner and serving customers such as Coca-Cola and GSK, bringing low-code, AI-powered tools into the platform to help HR and comms teams automate onboarding, engagement, learning, and recognition.
